Closing gaps left by prior works, we provide a sharp characterization of the thresholds governing how structural and contextual information interact in graph matching, and thereby establish a benchmark for designing efficient algorithms in the high-dimensional setting.

title: Locating a Seymour vertex in oriented graphs having minimum outdegree at most 7
abstract: A vertex $v$ of an oriented graph $D$ is a Seymour vertex if the number of outneighbors of $v$ is less than or equal to the number of second outneighbors of $v$ (vertices at directed distance exactly $2$ from $v$). Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture claims that every oriented graph contains a Seymour vertex. We propose the following stronger conjecture (Conjecture 1.4): given any oriented graphs $D$, there exists a minimum outdegree vertex $s$, and a Seymour vertex $v^*$ such that the directed distance from $s$ to $v^*$ is at most $\lfloor\frac{\delta^+(D)}{3} \rfloor$, where $\delta^+(D)$ denotes the minimum outdegree of $D$. The main contribution of this article is to show that Conjecture 1.4 is true for all oriented graphs having minimum outdegree at most $7$. This, in particular, improves the results of Kaneko and Locke (2001) which (implicitly) proved Conjecture 1.4 for all oriented graphs having minimum outdegree at most $6$. In particular, this yields Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture for this class of oriented graphs. We also construct a family of digraphs attaining the proposed distance bound, showing that it cannot be improved in general. Finally, by adapting existing arguments, we show that if Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture is true then given any oriented graph $D$ and any vertex $v$, it is always possible to find a Seymour vertex $v^*$ such that the directed distance from $v$ to $v^*$ is at most the outdegree of $v$.

title: From Mixing to Tearing: Graph Decomposition in Decentralized Optimization via Message Passing
abstract: We study decentralized minimization of sums of smooth strongly convex functions, one per agent, with communication restricted to neighbors in a graph. Existing decentralized algorithms typically emulate a {\it centralized} method; {\it the network serves only to exchange information}, from which agents approximate the global quantities that the method needs. This paper breaks with this paradigm. We introduce a {\it graph decomposition framework} that uses the network to design the method, not merely execute it. It jointly determines how agreement is imposed, which variables are optimized jointly (blocks), and which connected subgraphs host the agents solving each block. The convergence analysis quantifies the trade-offs among these choices. GATE (Graph-Tearing message passing) instantiates the framework by assigning one dual variable per edge and partitioning the edges into trees. Agents interleave edge updates with local message passing recursions that summarize optimization within each tree (block). Its surrogate variant, GATE-S, uses tractable local models and compact messages to reduce computation and communication. We establish linear convergence and show that the topology-aware design acts as a \emph{preconditioner}: the rate depends {\it jointly} on topology and function geometry through the coupling between subproblems defined on the selected subgraphs, whereas consensus-based optimization methods pay the worst case of each separately, the centralized condition number times the inverse spectral gap. On tree-dominant graphs, convergence is provably faster: the rate scales with the tree {\it diameter}, linearly in the number of agents on rings and barbells against quadratically for non-accelerated consensus-optimization methods. Experiments support the predicted scaling and savings in iterations and communication.

title: ProximalFM: Amortized Proximal Causal Inference under Hidden Confounding
abstract: Standard causal identification methods often assume no unmeasured confounding and can fail when relevant confounders are unobserved. Proximal causal inference instead uses proxy variables to identify effects under hidden confounding. However, nonparametric proximal estimation can be challenging in practice: recovering causal estimands such as the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) requires solving an ill-posed integral equation that is data-hungry, hyperparameter-sensitive, and optimization-unstable. Bayesian inference for such models provides a desirable alternative, mitigating these difficulties by regularizing through the prior. However, computing a posterior is itself challenging, as a typical likelihood function will include latent variables. Following the recent success of tabular foundation models in backdoor, instrumental variable, and frontdoor settings, we propose that prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are uniquely suited to resolve this bottleneck. Indeed, by training on synthetic data sampled from compliant structural causal models with access to oracle counterfactuals, we simplify the task substantially, amortizing the implied Bayesian operator inversion into a single transformer forward pass. Compared to prior literature that focuses primarily on point estimation, our model, ProximalFM, explicitly targets the Bayesian posterior distribution of the CATE. One unique aspect of this problem is that we need to provide Monte Carlo estimates of the oracle CATEs, leading to a novel variation of PFNs that accounts for the added stochastic error. Across a diverse suite of proximal regimes, ProximalFM achieves consistently strong CATE-estimation performance without dataset-specific tuning, with its largest advantage when latent confounding is substantial and the proxies are weakly informative; it also provides fast inference through a single amortized forward pass.
